stimulus:
Shards (use any, ignore the rest, let them collide):

- lichen: two kingdoms sharing one body; the boundary is the organism
- tide-pool desiccation, then sudden return of water
- a cathedral bell whose flaw gives it its pitch
- cuneiform tablets baked accidentally by the fire that destroyed the archive
- ant trail evaporating pheromone: memory that must be forgotten to function
- the sommelier's vocabulary: "flinty," "barnyard," "wet stone"
- error-correcting codes in DNA repair; a typo that is also a signature
- potlatch: status gained by destroying wealth
- moiré: two regular grids producing a pattern neither contains
- the negative space between roots
- a ferry timetable written for passengers who never arrive
- mycelial relay: the slowest network, the longest memory
- kintsugi, but for a broken measurement
- the quiet minute after an earthquake when dogs already knew
- pidgin becoming creole in one generation of children
- a lock that only opens when slightly wrong key is used
- the amateur's blunder that a veteran has trained away
- sandpile avalanches: the same grain, a different cause each time

Instruction to self: before answering, pick two shards that feel least related to the question. Force a structural analogy from each: what is the mechanism, what is inverted, what is being kept because it is flawed, what is being forgotten on purpose? Propose ideas that import those mechanisms, and avoid the first three ideas that come to mind.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Pheromone-evaporation test: AP-1 decay kinetics vs. memory persistence
ideas.description: After a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, wounding, or cytokine pulse), measure the half-lives of AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN/ChIP time course, live-cell FOS/JUN reporters) and of the chromatin accessibility it created (ATAC-seq), then use acute degron removal (dTAG on FOS/JUN) at varied delays to test whether the memory is held by AP-1 itself or persists once it is gone. Memory that requires continuous AP-1 behaves like a trail needing constant renewal, whereas memory that persists after AP-1 removal is self-sustaining. The 'forgetting' rate is then compared with the rate at which re-stimulation response is lost.

ideas.title: Desiccation-and-rewatering primed-response assay with single-cell multiome
ideas.description: Give cells a first stimulus, let them return to baseline for days (the 'dry' phase), then deliver a second stimulus and measure the primed response by scRNA+ATAC multiome, comparing naive, primed, and AP-1 dominant-negative (A-FOS) or degron-treated cells. Test whether the faster or stronger second response depends on AP-1 sites that stayed open as 'latent' accessible elements, and whether the dependence is cell-autonomous by tracking lineages via barcodes across division.

ideas.title: Moiré combinatorics: dimer-composition code across two input grids
ideas.description: AP-1 dimers (FOS/JUN/ATF/MAF families) combine with partner TFs (e.g., ETS, NFAT, lineage TFs) to produce composite motifs. Use paired perturbation of dimer composition and partner presence (CRISPRi/degron matrix) with ChIP/CUT&Tag and MPRA to test whether history is encoded in which dimer and partner pairs were engaged — a pattern neither input contains alone. Predict that a history-specific dimer/partner signature at enhancers can decode a cell's past stimulus from chromatin state with a classifier trained on known histories.

ideas.title: Kintsugi of a flawed reporter: using imperfect AP-1 sites as memory switches
ideas.description: Use CRISPR base-editing or saturation mutagenesis of AP-1 motifs at a memory-associated enhancer to create variants with weakened (flawed) affinity, then test whether the suboptimal sites are the ones that retain memory, e.g., by sustaining accessibility with slow decay, while consensus TRE sites respond quickly and forget. Quantify with MPRA and locus-specific live imaging (dCas9 or reporter) across stimulus histories. This asks whether imperfection in motif affinity is what gives hysteresis, like a bell flaw setting its pitch.

ideas.title: Sandpile-style dose-history mapping: same factor, different causes
ideas.description: Apply stimuli of different types (mechanical, inflammatory, growth factor, injury) with systematically varied intensity, duration, and spacing, and measure induced AP-1 composition, enhancer occupancy, and downstream gene state with time-resolved CUT&Tag and RNA-seq. Fit a dynamical (bistability/hysteresis) model to ask whether AP-1 'avalanche' responses show threshold, history-dependent state transitions, and avalanche-size distributions that differ by stimulus cause even though the same factor is activated. Validate by predicting the outcome of untested stimulus sequences.
